feat(input): map AYANEO Pocket DS extra buttons on ayaneo_mcu_xbox

Enroll the AYANEO Pocket DS's front menu keys and back paddles.

The Pocket DS matches `01-ayaneo-controller.yaml`, which uses the
shared `ayaneo_mcu_xbox` capability map. Prior to this patch, only
the standard face/shoulder/trigger/stick buttons and BTN_MODE were
mapped; the Aya button, the redundant Steam button, and both L4/L5
+ R4/R5 back paddles were dropped by InputPlumber.

Verified empirically on hardware (Pocket DS running Armada 7.0.11
aarch64). Capture used the accompanying ipcap tool
(https://github.com/pacoa-kdbg/inputplumber-capture-suite) with
InputPlumber temporarily stopped; each button was pressed once
after another and every press produced exactly one MCU event on
event3:

    Aya            -> KEY BTN5 (261) + MSC_SCAN=0x90006
    Steam button   -> KEY BTN2 (258) + MSC_SCAN=0x90003
    L4             -> KEY BTN3 (259) + MSC_SCAN=0x90004
    R4             -> KEY BTN4 (260) + MSC_SCAN=0x90005
    L5             -> KEY BTN7 (263) + MSC_SCAN=0x90008
    R5             -> KEY BTN6 (262) + MSC_SCAN=0x90007

Mappings:
  * `BTN5`  -> `gamepad.QuickAccess`  (was `keyboard.KeyF1`, wrong
                                       target for a QAM key)
  * `BTN2`  -> `gamepad.Guide`        (redundant with BTN_MODE from
                                       the composite gamepad)
  * `BTN3`  -> `gamepad.LeftPaddle1`
  * `BTN4`  -> `gamepad.RightPaddle1`
  * `BTN7`  -> `gamepad.LeftPaddle2`
  * `BTN6`  -> `gamepad.RightPaddle2`

The existing `BTN_C -> RightPaddle1` and `BTN_Z -> LeftPaddle1`
mappings are preserved untouched; they route the older AYANEO
paddle hardware that emits those codes. Devices that only emit
BTN3/BTN4 (like the DS) now reach the same target without any
change to the pre-existing mapping for other AYANEO models.

Testing:
  * Installed as `/etc/inputplumber/capability_maps.d/
    ayaneo_mcu_xbox.yaml` runtime override on the Pocket DS.
  * `systemctl restart inputplumber` re-matched `01-ayaneo-
    controller.yaml` cleanly (see journal below).
  * In-game verification in Steam Big Picture: Aya opens QAM
    sidebar; Steam button opens Steam UI (redundant with Guide);
    L4/L5/R4/R5 each register on their target paddle slot.
  * No regressions observed on standard face buttons (BTN_SOUTH/
    _EAST/_NORTH/_WEST), shoulders (BTN_TL/_TR), triggers
    (ABS_Z/ABS_RZ), sticks (ABS_X/_Y/_RX/_RY), or D-pad
    (ABS_HAT0X/Y).

Journal excerpt after restart:
    inputplumber::input::manager] Found a matching input device
    evdev://event3 in config "/usr/share/inputplumber/devices/
    01-ayaneo-controller.yaml", creating CompositeDevice
    inputplumber::input::composite_device] Loading device profile
    `Default` from: /usr/share/inputplumber/profiles/default.yaml

Related devices:
  * AYANEO Pocket EVO, Pocket DS, and Pocket S 2K all match this
    same config/map pair. Only the DS was hardware-verified; the
    other two use the identical MCU family and should benefit
    from the same mapping without further change, but they remain
    formally untested here.

fix(input): route AYANEO MCU japanese-layout QAM+paddles to gamepad

The `ayaneo_mcu_japanese` capability map previously routed the front
QAM key to `keyboard.KeyF1`, which prevents Steam from surfacing its
Quick Access Menu overlay on AYANEO handhelds that use the japanese
device configuration (Pocket ACE, Pocket DMG). It also dropped every
non-Guide MCU button (paddles, secondary front keys) silently.

This patch:

1. Fixes the QAM key: routes `BTN5 + MSC_SCAN=0x90006` to
   `gamepad.QuickAccess` (was `keyboard.KeyF1`).

2. Enrolls four back-paddle buttons:
   * L4 `BTN3` + MSC 0x90004 -> `gamepad.LeftPaddle1`
   * R4 `BTN4` + MSC 0x90005 -> `gamepad.RightPaddle1`
   * L5 `BTN7` + MSC 0x90008 -> `gamepad.LeftPaddle2`
   * R5 `BTN6` + MSC 0x90007 -> `gamepad.RightPaddle2`
     (R5 is the physical "Aya" secondary front button.)

Verified empirically on hardware (Pocket ACE running Armada 7.0.11
aarch64, InputPlumber v0.77.2). Capture used the accompanying ipcap
tool (https://github.com/pacoa-kdbg/inputplumber-capture-suite v0.3.0)
with InputPlumber temporarily stopped so the raw evdev nodes could
be read directly. Each button was pressed once in a strict order and
every press produced exactly one MCU event on event3 (the AYANEO
DEVICE keyboard, `1c4f:0002`).

Testing:
  * Installed as `/etc/inputplumber/capability_maps.d/
    ayaneo_mcu_japanese.yaml` runtime override on the Pocket ACE.
  * `systemctl restart inputplumber` re-matched
    `01-ayaneo-controller-japanese.yaml` cleanly.
  * In-game verification in Steam Big Picture: QAM opens sidebar;
    L4/L5/R4/R5 each register as their paddle slot on the virtual
    xb360 pad; no regressions on standard face buttons, shoulders,
    triggers, sticks, or D-pad.

Compatibility with other AYANEO devices sharing this cap map:
The pre-existing `BTN_C -> RightPaddle1` and `BTN_Z -> LeftPaddle1`
entries are preserved; those source codes are what older AYANEO
paddle firmware emits. Devices whose MCU only emits BTN3/BTN4
(the current japanese-family hardware line) reach the same target
without breaking older devices.

Pocket DMG uses the same `01-ayaneo-controller-japanese.yaml`
device match and therefore the same `ayaneo_mcu_japanese`
capability map. It shares the same MCU family as the ACE and is
expected to work identically with this patch, but remains formally
untested here (kept as `Untested` in README).

Add AYN Thor second screen support (userspace)

With the bottom panel enabled in the kernel, the top screen becomes
DSI-2 and a second backlight (ae94000.dsi.0) appears that Steam picks
up for brightness control instead of the top panel's.

- ayn-thor.conf: primary connector is DSI-2; declare the primary
  backlight, secondary connector, and both touchscreen device names
- steamos-priv-write: accept backlight brightness writes and steer them
  to ARMADA_PRIMARY_BACKLIGHT, rescaling between brightness ranges
  (bottom is 0-255, top is 0-4096)
- desktop-bootstrap/setup-dual-screen: one-time desktop layout for
  dual-screen devices - primary on top at priority 1, secondary
  centered below, each touchscreen pinned to its own output (KWin
  otherwise maps both to the same screen)

Requires the armada-packages kernel with the Thor bottom panel enabled;
on the old kernel DSI-2 does not exist and gamescope falls back to the
only connected output, so ordering is safe.

setup-dual-screen: tolerate trailing text in kscreen-doctor JSON

kscreen-doctor -o -j prints the human-readable listing after the JSON
document, so json.loads raised JSONDecodeError and the script died
before applying the layout or pinning the touchscreens. On first boot
that left both touchscreens mapped to the same output: taps on the top
screen landed on the bottom desktop, where a stray double-tap on the
Return to Game Mode icon logged the session out.

Request JSON alone and parse only the first document so trailing text
can never take the script down again. Verified on an AYN Thor: layout
applied, both touchscreens pinned to their own panel.

Withhold direct backlight access on dual-screen devices

The perf-ACL udev rule made every backlight's brightness group-writable,
so Steam's direct sysfs write (its first choice before falling back to
steamos-polkit-helpers/steamos-priv-write) succeeded on whichever
backlight it enumerated first - on Thor the secondary bottom panel. The
priv-write steering to ARMADA_PRIMARY_BACKLIGHT never engaged except for
out-of-range values, so the brightness slider dimmed the desktop screen
instead of the gaming one.

Observed on hardware: at Steam startup a saved 0-4096-scale value hit the
255-max bottom panel (EINVAL, then rescaled to 166 and correctly steered
2666 -> top panel via priv-write), but ordinary slider writes were
in-range for the bottom panel and landed there directly.

The udev grant now goes through backlight-acl, which withholds it from
every backlight when ARMADA_PRIMARY_BACKLIGHT is set: all Steam writes
fail EACCES and funnel through the steering helper, the same path Steam
uses on stock SteamOS where backlight sysfs is not user-writable.
Single-backlight devices keep the direct grant.

Fire wedged-controller repair when an unrelated pad left WINEXINPUT keys

repair_wedged_controller() treated any WINEXINPUT key anywhere in system.reg
as proof the pad had promoted, and returned early. Those keys outlive the
device that created them, so a prefix carrying WINEXINPUT\VID_045E&PID_028E
left over from an xb360 target suppressed the repair for the unrelated
VID_28DE pad - short-circuiting on exactly the corrupted prefixes the fixup
exists to clean up.

This is reachable on AYANEO devices, where InputPlumber builds the composite
as xb360 before armada-controller-type re-targets it to deck-uhid at boot,
seeding VID_045E keys that persist in every prefix created afterwards. AYN
devices boot straight to deck-uhid and never seed them.

Symptom on a Pocket EVO: the pad reaches the prefix (lnxev_device_create,
is_gamepad 1) but registration collides on every launch -

  err:plugplay:enumerate_new_device Failed to create or open device
  L"USB\VID_28DE&PID_11FF&MI_00\0&00000000000011ff28de&0&0&1", error 0xe000020b

The instance ID is derived from VID/PID, so the collision is deterministic
and the prefix never self-heals. Games poll XInput indices 0-3 indefinitely
and receive nothing. Confirmed on Crash N-Sane Trilogy and DOOM 2016;
scoping the check to the same pad makes the repair fire and restores input.

Map Pocket EVO AYA SPACE, =, LC and RC buttons

These four buttons are wired to SoC GPIOs rather than to the controller
MCU, so they never appear on the fake-Xbox-360 pad and were unmapped.
They arrive instead on their own gpio-keys node, which the kernel only
creates once the device tree declares it.

Kept out of the existing gpio-keys node deliberately: InputPlumber grabs
the source devices it manages, so sharing that node would swallow volume
up.

The device tree emits F13-F16 rather than AYANEO's stock KEY_A,
KEY_EQUAL, KEY_LEFT and KEY_RIGHTSHIFT. Those type real characters, so
any moment InputPlumber is not grabbing the node - desktop mode, a
service restart - they would leak into whatever has focus.

Only AYA SPACE is bound to a fixed action, since QuickAccess is the one
thing Steam Input cannot bind. The other three become paddles so they
stay remappable per game.

Needs the matching aya-keys node in qcs8550-ayaneo-pocketevo.dts; until
that lands nothing matches "aya-keys" and this config is inert.

Verified on hardware by patching the DTB in place and reading the
emulated Steam Controller's HID reports: AYA SPACE opens QAM, and =, LC
and RC report as L5, L4 and R4.

Mask the IPCC mailbox IRQ on suspend for SM8550 too

0504 currently drops IRQF_NO_SUSPEND only when the IPCC node is
"qcom,sm8750-ipcc", so SM8550 still requests the summary interrupt with
IRQF_NO_SUSPEND and it is never masked across suspend.

On SM8550 the ADSP charger firmware pushes an unsolicited
BATTMGR_NOTIFICATION roughly half a second after suspend entry. With the
mailbox irq unmasked that notification pulls the SoC straight back out,
which upstream ROCKNIX identifies as the single biggest blocker to SM8550
staying asleep.

Extend the existing compatible check to cover "qcom,sm8550-ipcc". Every
other SoC keeps IRQF_NO_SUSPEND, so established behavior on the shared
driver is unchanged.

This is the same fix ROCKNIX merged in PR #3115, which removes the flag
unconditionally; keeping armada's compatible gate preserves the existing
caution for SM8250 and SM8650.

No behavior change on current builds: every SM8550 device here runs
ARMADA_SUSPEND_MODE=fake, so the system never reaches a real suspend where
the flag matters. This is groundwork for when SM8550 suspend is enabled.

Upgrade to Linux 7.2 rc7 with minimal SM8550 sleep fixes

Fix the RP6 touchscreen sampling rate (28 Hz to 119 Hz)

The RP6 touchscreen reports at ~28 Hz while the same panel runs at
~119 Hz under the vendor Android kernel.

The controller is programmed identically on both: report rate register
0x88 = 12 (120 Hz). The difference is entirely in how the frame is read.
`no-regmap-bulk-read` makes edt-ft5x06 fetch the touch frame one byte at
a time; for focaltech,ft5426 that is tdata_len = 6 * 10 + 3 = 63 separate
I2C transactions per interrupt.

Measured on the device over /dev/i2c-1 at the stock 100 kHz:

  63 x 1-byte reads   35.30 ms/frame  ->   28.3 Hz ceiling
  1 x 63-byte read     6.31 ms/frame  ->  158.4 Hz ceiling

The measured evdev rate was 28.6 Hz and the touch IRQ fired ~28.5 times a
second, i.e. the per-byte read time *is* the sample rate: the handler
takes far longer than the controller's 8.33 ms report period, so
edge-triggered interrupts are missed.

The workaround was introduced for AYN SM8550 hardware ("problem with
regmap_bulk_read under i2c_hub_*") and the RP6 inherited it. It is not
needed here -- 200 consecutive 63-byte bulk reads on this bus complete
without a single failure, and crc_errors/header_errors stay at 0.

Also raise the bus to 400 kHz. At 100 kHz a bulk read still occupies
6.31 ms of every 8.33 ms frame (76%), leaving no margin under load; at
400 kHz it takes 1.72 ms (21%). Every other Armada device using this
controller (AYANEO Pocket EVO/DS, AYN Odin3) already runs 400 kHz.

After the change, measured on hardware: 8.416 ms median frame interval
(118.8 Hz) against Android's 8.407 ms (118.9 Hz), touch IRQ steady at
120/s, crc_errors and header_errors still 0.

Note: qcs8550-ayn-thor.dts carries the same combination and is likely
affected the same way (ft5452, 33-byte frame -> ~54 Hz). Left alone here
since it is untested -- the original workaround was written for AYN
hardware, so it may be load-bearing there.

fix(kernel): correct SM8250 Type-C VBUS and SBU routing

Wire the PM8150B VBUS regulator to the USB-C connector and model the board's discrete GPIO-controlled SBU/AUX mux.

The previous device tree routed the SBU endpoint through the NB7VPQ904M and assigned TLMM9 as the redriver enable GPIO. On this hardware, TLMM8 selects the SBU/AUX orientation and TLMM9 enables the separate SBU mux.

This caused DisplayPort AUX communication to fail when the USB-C plug was inserted in the reversed orientation. HPD and DP Alt Mode were active, but DRM remained disconnected and no EDID could be read.

Add a gpio-sbu-mux using TLMM8/TLMM9, move the Type-C SBU graph connection to it, and leave the NB7VPQ904M responsible for the high-speed path.

Also add the missing vbus-supply reference to pm8150b_vbus so the Qualcomm Type-C controller uses the real VBUS regulator instead of a dummy regulator.

Tested on Retroid Pocket Flip 2 (SM8250), Linux 7.2.3:
normal orientation: connected, 256-byte EDID
reverse orientation: connected, 256-byte EDID
